sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Concept
sections.content: The Accommodative Convergence/Accommodation (AC/A) ratio represents the amount of accommodative convergence (measured in prism diopters, Δ) that occurs for every unit of accommodation (measured in diopters, D) exerted. It is a critical metric for diagnosing and managing non-strabismic binocular vision anomalies and pediatric esotropia. A normal ratio typically ranges from 3:1 to 5:1.

sections.title: The Heterophoria Method
content: Step 1: Measure Interpupillary Distance (PD) in centimeters.
Step 2: Measure Near Deviation (Dn) and Distance Deviation (Df) in prism diopters.
Step 3: Note: Esophoria (+) and Exophoria (-).
Step 4: Use Formula: AC/A = PD + [(Dn - Df) / A], where A is the accommodative stimulus at near (usually 3.0D or 4.0D).
Note: This method includes the effect of proximal accommodation.

sections.title: The Gradient Method
content: Step 1: Measure baseline deviation at a fixed distance (usually 6m or 33cm).
Step 2: Place a lens (usually -2.00D or +3.00D) in front of the eyes.
Step 3: Re-measure the deviation with the lenses in place.
Step 4: Use Formula: AC/A = (Deviation with lens - Baseline deviation) / Lens Power.
Note: This method eliminates proximal accommodation and is often more clinically relevant for bifocal prescription.

sections.title: Management Strategy: High AC/A ET
content: 1. Full Cycloplegic Refraction: Mandatory in all cases.
2. Full Hyperopic Correction: Prescribe the maximum tolerated.
3. Bifocals: Executive or flat-top (line at lower pupillary margin) if residual ET at near.
4. Miotics: Echothiophate iodide 0.125% (if bifocals not tolerated).
5. Surgery: Indicated if non-accommodative component remains >15Δ.

sections.title: Management Strategy: Low AC/A CI
content: 1. Orthoptics/Vision Therapy: Pencil push-ups, Brock string, Computer-based orthoptics.
2. Prism: Base-in (BI) prisms for reading (Relieving prisms).
3. Minus Lenses: To stimulate accommodative convergence (rarely used).
4. CITT Study: Proven superiority of office-based therapy over home-based therapy.

sections.title: Pharmacological Modulation
content: Miotics (Echothiophate Iodide / Phospholine Iodide) lower the AC/A ratio.
Mechanism: Induces 'peripheral' accommodation, requiring less central effort.
Risk: Iris cysts (prevented by 2.5% phenylephrine).
Atropine: Can indirectly increase AC/A by forcing more central effort.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: High AC/A Risks
content: Sudden onset esotropia in older children (Rule out CNS tumor).
Bifocal fit too low (Line must bisect pupil in children).
Iris cysts from Miotic use.
Post-surgical exotropia in high AC/A patients.

content.explanation: Convergence Excess = High AC/A | Convergence Insufficiency = Low AC/A.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: AC/A ratio remains stable throughout life until the onset of presbyopia.
Patients with High AC/A ET are more prone to consecutive exotropia after surgery.
Simulated Divergence Excess: High AC/A that masquerades as true DE; use +3.00D lenses or patch test to differentiate.
Bifocals should only be used if they restore binocularity/fusion at near.

rows: Fully corrected by full hyperopic correction at D & N

Residual ET despite correction and/or bifocals

sections.title: Recent Advances: The CITT Study
sections.content: The Convergence Insufficiency Treatment Trial (CITT) provided landmark evidence that office-based vergence-accommodative therapy is significantly more effective than home-based therapy or pencil push-ups for symptomatic CI in children. For High AC/A, recent studies on Progressive Addition Lenses (PALs) show they are a viable alternative to traditional flat-top bifocals, though adherence and positioning are critical.
